tA.text: A · Sheet: reading-first, Ultimate Guitar style

nA.text:
Best for: learning a new song at a desk, reading ahead like a printed chart. The chart is the hero; player, keyboard and controls stay slim at the edges. Chord diagrams pop over on hover, and a strip lists every chord in the song.

Tradeoffs: the current chord is small, so glancing up mid-song means finding your place again. The keyboard drawer costs height on a laptop. Inline editing is quick for 2 or 3 wrong chords, slow for a badly detected song or timing fixes.

tB.text: B · Stage: performance-first, Chordify / Moises style

nB.text:
Best for: playing along with hands on the keys and eyes up, laptop or phone on the music rest. One huge chord, the next one counting in, a full-width 32-key piano, and lyrics as karaoke.

Tradeoffs: only 2 lyric lines show, so you see less of the song's structure and can't read far ahead. Editing is pause-and-fix with the detector's other guesses: great for one wrong chord, clumsy for fixing timing across a whole song. The key wheel is playful but takes space.

nC.text:
Best for: cleaning up detection right after import (70 to 85% accuracy means several wrong chords per song). Waveform timeline, draggable chord blocks with snap-to-beat, a review queue of unsure chords, and edit history.

Tradeoffs: the busiest screen, and desktop-first: on a phone it shrinks to one lane plus a bottom sheet. Weakest for playing along. Likely best as the edit mode inside A or B rather than a whole app.

nP.text: Shared by all three directions. Orange keys = play now (with note names). Blue dots = the next chord, so you can prepare the hand move. Small C labels mark each octave. Range matches the Casio SA-51: F3 to C6.
